chapter_theme: The book opens by rooting ஆசாரம் in eight ethical virtues and promising its rewards, then sets out the rules of the period for the day: rising and worship, the kinds of எச்சில் and what they bar, the occasions and manner of bathing, reverence owed to elders and sacred things, and the purifying acts and posture of the meal.
structure_note: Verses 1-3 frame conduct ethically; 4 and 9 give the morning; 5-8 define எச்சில் and its bars; 10-14 bathing, dress and oil; 15-17 reverence and calendar rules; 18-20 the meal.

1.reading: The verse names eight things as the seed from which the conduct called ஆசாரம் grows: gratitude, forbearance, sweet speech, doing nothing painful to any living being, learning, knowing how to do oppuravu fully, wisdom, and friendship with good company.
1.nuance: The book that goes on to list rules of bathing and eating opens by rooting them in inner virtues; வித்து makes the ritual rules the plant and the ethics the seed, so the order of the work is itself a claim.

items.claim: knowing a kindness received is a seed of ஆசாரம்
having forbearance is a seed of ஆசாரம்
sweet speech is a seed of ஆசாரம்
not doing painful things to any living being is a seed of ஆசாரம்
learning is a seed of ஆசாரம்
knowing how to carry out oppuravu, help to the community, in full is a seed of ஆசாரம்
possessing wisdom is a seed of ஆசாரம்
making friends with those of good company is a seed of ஆசாரம்

2.reading: The verse says that those who never fail in conduct gain eight things by right: good birth, long life, wealth, beauty, ownership of land, high renown, learning and freedom from disease.
2.nuance: Birth heads the list of rewards, so good birth is treated as something conduct earns, presumably in a later life, rather than as the ground of conduct; the verse does not say which life the eight arrive in. ஒழக்கம் on line 4 is read as ஒழுக்கம்.

items.claim: good birth is gained by those who never fail in conduct
long life is gained by them
wealth is gained by them
beauty is gained by them
lordship over land is gained by them
high renown is gained by them
learning is gained by them
freedom from disease is gained by them

3.reading: The verse says that gifts to priests, sacrifice, penance and learning are to be kept and carried through by the threefold discipline, and that if they are not, they come to nothing on any side and perish.
3.domain_note: the man who gives fees and performs sacrifice
3.nuance: முப்பால் ஒழுக்கு is not explained in the verse; it can be the discipline of mind, speech and body, or conduct in the three aims of aram, porul and inbam. On either reading the claim is that rite and penance are void without conduct to hold them.

items.claim: the gift to priests perishes unless guarded by threefold conduct
sacrifice perishes unless guarded by threefold conduct
penance perishes unless guarded by threefold conduct
learning perishes unless guarded by threefold conduct

norm.note: a rule of the period on the Vedic acts of fee-giving and sacrifice and how they are kept fruitful

4.reading: The verse reports the order the ancients saw: to wake in the last watch before dawn, think over the good deeds and the honest wealth one will pursue that day, and rise worshipping father and mother.
4.nuance: Aram and porul are planned before rising, and the first act of worship is to the parents, not to a god. வாய்வதில் on line 2 is not clear to me; it may mean 'in what is fitting' or 'as far as it comes to hand'.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period: the hour of waking and the first act of the day

5.reading: The verse lists five things that, it says, no one in a state of எச்சில் touches: the cow, brahmins, fire, the gods and the crown of one's own head.
5.nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a birth-group term; the verse sets brahmins beside the cow, fire and the gods as things an impure hand must not reach, so the rule ranks people by birth as well as regulating purity. The crown of the head is the one item on one's own body.

items.claim: the cow is not touched by one in எச்சில்
brahmins are not touched by one in எச்சில்
fire is not touched by one in எச்சில்
the gods are not touched by one in எச்சில்
the crown of the head is not touched by one in எச்சில்

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: what the unclean hand is barred from touching, with brahmins ranked among sacred things

6.reading: The verse lists five things those in a state of எச்சில் do not look at: புலை, the moon, the sun, a dog and a falling star, and says those who know this well keep it daily and promptly.
6.nuance: புலை is a caste term here most likely naming the outcaste person, set in a list with a dog and the heavenly bodies as sights barred to the unclean; it could also be read as an impure thing such as flesh, which is why the verse is marked uncertain. தக்கவீழ் மீன் is read as a falling star.

items.claim: the outcaste person, or on another reading an impure thing, is not looked at by one in எச்சில்
the moon is not looked at by one in எச்சில்
the sun is not looked at by one in எச்சில்
a dog is not looked at by one in எச்சில்
a falling star is not looked at by one in எச்சில்

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: what is barred from sight while the mouth is unclean, with a birth-group among the barred sights

7.reading: The verse says there are many kinds of எச்சில் and singles out four: the two excretions, sexual union and the mouth's desire, eating.
7.nuance: The count of four is reached by taking இயக்கம் இரண்டும் as two (urine and faeces), so three items are listed here; வாயின் விழைச்சு is read as eating. Eating, the body's most ordinary act, is put in the same class as excretion and intercourse.

items.claim: the two excretions are each a kind of எச்சில், counted as two
sexual union is a kind of எச்சில்
the mouth's desire, eating, is a kind of எச்சில்

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: the classes of bodily act that make a person unclean

8.reading: The verse says those who would become learned observe the four kinds of எச்சில் carefully and never recite, speak or lie down to sleep while in them.
8.nuance: The reward named is மேதை, learning or brilliance, not merit: keeping the purity rules is tied to the power of recitation. வளரார் is read as 'do not lie down to sleep'.

items.claim: one in எச்சில் does not recite
one in எச்சில் does not speak
one in எச்சில் does not lie down to sleep

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: recitation and speech barred while unclean

9.reading: The verse sets the morning rite: at dawn twilight one chews the tooth-stick, washes the eyes and rises after worshipping the deity in the way one knows, and it calls worship standing at evening twilight a fault.
9.nuance: தானறியும் ஆற்றால் leaves the form of worship and the deity to the worshipper; only the hour and the posture are fixed.

norm.note: an order-of-the-day rule of the period: cleansing and worship at the two twilights

10.reading: The verse lists ten occasions on which, it says, one bathes without hesitation: worship of the gods, a bad dream, uncleanness, vomiting what one has eaten, cutting the hair, mealtime, rising from sleep, sexual union, bodily contact with low people, and the other, falling into confusion.
10.nuance: Ten is reached by taking ஊண்பொழுது and வைகு துயில் as two occasions; ஏனை மயலுறல் is obscure and may mean any other bewilderment. கீழ்மக்கள் can be a moral term (the base), as often in the Kural, but a contact that calls for a bath points to a birth-group, so it is read as a caste term here. வாலாமை, uncleanness, may include menstrual or death pollution; the verse does not say whose.

items.claim: worship of the gods calls for a bath
a bad dream calls for a bath
a state of uncleanness calls for a bath
vomiting what one has eaten calls for a bath
cutting the hair calls for a bath
the time of the meal calls for a bath
rising from sleep calls for a bath
sexual union calls for a bath
touching the body of low people calls for a bath
the other, falling into confusion, calls for a bath

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period: the occasions that require bathing, one of them contact with a ranked group

11.reading: The verse reports the ancients' rule that the worthy do not bathe unclothed, do not eat wearing a single cloth, do not wring the cloth they wear inside the water, and never enter an assembly in a single cloth.
11.nuance: உடுத்தலால் is read as உடுத்து அலால், 'except clothed'. The single-cloth rule joins the meal and the assembly, so dress is a matter of both purity and public standing.

items.claim: the worthy do not bathe except clothed
the worthy do not eat in a single cloth
the worthy do not wring the worn cloth in the water
the worthy do not enter the assembly in a single cloth

norm.note: a rule of the period on dress at bathing, eating and in the assembly

12.reading: The verse says the worthy do not touch any limb with the oil rubbed on the head, do not touch the soiled cloth another has worn, and do not beg for sandals even when they lack them.
12.nuance: The last item moves from pollution to self-respect: a want as small as sandals does not license begging, so the verse joins bodily purity and the refusal to ask.

items.claim: oil rubbed on the head is not used to touch another limb
the soiled cloth another wore is not touched
sandals are not got by begging even when lacking

norm.note: a rule of the period on oil and others' worn cloth as sources of uncleanness

13.reading: The verse lists things the worthy avoid: gazing at their reflection in water, scratching the ground at night, going near trees at night, rubbing on oil without first touching water even in distress, and, once oiled, touching water or looking at புலை.
13.nuance: The order of oil and water on lines 3-4 is hard to fix: one reading is that water is touched before oiling and not again after, until the bath. புலை is again a caste term most likely naming the outcaste person, though it could be an impure thing; the bar on seeing it here attaches to the oiled state, not to எச்சில்.

items.claim: the worthy do not gaze at their reflection in water
the worthy do not scratch the ground at night
the worthy do not go near trees at night
the worthy do not rub on oil without touching water, even in distress
once oiled, the worthy do not touch water
once oiled, the worthy do not look at புலை

norm.note: a pollution rule of the period on night, oil and water, with a birth-group among the barred sights

14.reading: The verse says that those who keep the path never, while bathing, swim, spit, splash about or play, and do not bathe leaving out the head even when it is dry.
14.nuance: The ritual bath is set against the bath as pleasure: every banned act is play in water. காய்ந்தது எனினும் is read as 'even if the head is dry'; it could also mean 'even if the water is cold'.

items.claim: they do not swim while bathing
they do not spit while bathing
they do not splash about while bathing
they do not play while bathing
they do not bathe leaving out the head

norm.note: a rule of the period on the manner of the purifying bath

15.reading: The verse says that one who scorns the five elements, brahmins, the cow, the moon and the sun, not reckoning them as his own elements, has the five elements of his own body perish at once.
15.nuance: தம்பூதம் makes the outer things kin to the elements of the body, so contempt for them is self-destruction. பார்ப்பார் is a birth-group term, and the verse places brahmins among cosmic and sacred things owed reverence by birth.

items.claim: the five elements are not to be scorned
brahmins are not to be scorned
the cow is not to be scorned
the moon is not to be scorned
the sun is not to be scorned

norm.note: a rule of the period that ranks brahmins by birth among things owed reverence

16.reading: The verse names the king, the teacher, the mother, the father and the elder brother as the peerless elders, and reports as the way all have seen that they are to be worshipped as gods.
16.nuance: The king heads a list otherwise made of household and teacher, so political and family authority are given one kind of reverence; the wife's duty to the husband, which the Kural treats this way, is not among them.

items.claim: the king is a peerless elder to be worshipped as a god
the teacher is a peerless elder to be worshipped as a god
the mother is a peerless elder to be worshipped as a god
the father is a peerless elder to be worshipped as a god
the elder brother is a peerless elder to be worshipped as a god

17.reading: The verse gives the settled view of the wise: they do not act against their elders' word, do not forget to complete vows left unfinished, do not chew the tooth-stick on the full-moon day, and do not cut trees.
17.nuance: நிறையுவா மேல் may mean the full-moon day and the days after it, or the full and new moon; and the tree-cutting bar may belong to the same day or stand alone. The list joins obedience, vows and calendar rules as one kind of thing.

items.claim: the wise do not act against their elders' word
the wise do not forget to complete unfinished vows
the wise do not chew the tooth-stick on the full-moon day
the wise do not cut trees

norm.note: a calendar and vow rule of the period

18.reading: The verse says that only those who eat after bathing, washing the feet, rinsing the mouth and drawing the circle on the ground are said to have eaten; the others, rinsing their mouths as if they had eaten, go off, and the rakshasas, resenting this, take their meal as their own.
18.nuance: The sanction is not illness or sin but theft: an unritualed meal is not eaten by the eater at all, because demons claim it. மண்டலஞ்செய்து is read as marking the circle for the leaf.

items.claim: bathing before the meal makes it truly eaten
washing the feet before the meal makes it truly eaten
rinsing the mouth before the meal makes it truly eaten
drawing the circle before the meal makes it truly eaten

norm.note: a rule of the period on the purifying acts before a meal

19.reading: The verse reports the settled view of the very wise that one eats before the water on the feet has dried, and does not climb into bed before the wetness has dried.
19.nuance: The same wet feet are required for the meal and forbidden for the bed; the rule turns on timing, not on water as such.

items.claim: one eats while the feet are still wet
one does not climb into bed while still wet

norm.note: a rule of the period on wet feet at meal and bed

20.reading: The verse sets the posture of the meal: one faces east, sits well, does not doze or sway, looks at nothing else and does not speak, and eats after worship, carefully, without spilling.
20.nuance: Every item governs the eater's body and attention; none governs the food, its amount or its kind.

items.claim: the direction faced while eating is east
the eater does not doze
the eater does not sway
the eater looks at nothing else
the eater does not speak
the eater eats after worship
the eater does not spill

norm.note: a rule of the period on direction, posture and silence at the meal

links.note: Kural 131 puts ஒழுக்கம் above life because it gives excellence; Acharakkovai 1 says what conduct grows from, naming eight inner virtues as its seed.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kural's command to guard conduct gets a source: the conduct to be guarded is not a set of rules but the outgrowth of gratitude, patience and the rest.
links.list_adds: It makes rule-bound conduct the fruit of eight ethical virtues, so a ritual code is founded on ethics before any ritual rule is given.

links.note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and its lapse is low birth; Acharakkovai 2 makes good birth one of eight rewards that unfailing conduct earns.
links.teaches: Both tie birth to conduct, but the Kural collapses birth into present conduct while the Acharakkovai keeps birth as a real rank that conduct earns, so the same link can dissolve or confirm hierarchy.
links.list_adds: It sets birth among worldly rewards such as wealth, land and health, so birth becomes a prize of conduct rather than its definition.

links.note: Acharakkovai 3 lists sacrifice among four acts to be guarded and kept fruitful; Kural 259 rates abstaining from killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices.
links.teaches: The ritual code keeps sacrifice as a thing of value needing protection by conduct, while the Kural prices it below a single act of non-killing, so the two books weigh the same rite very differently.
links.list_adds: It groups sacrifice with fees, penance and learning as goods that conduct preserves, where the Kural sets sacrifice against non-killing and ranks it lower.

links.note: Verse 4 has one rise worshipping father and mother; verse 16 names five elders, parents among them, to be worshipped as gods.
links.teaches: Verse 16 supplies the rank that verse 4's daily act presupposes, and shows the dawn rite honours only two of the five elders owed god-like worship.

links.note: Acharakkovai 5 bars one in எச்சில் from touching brahmins and other sacred things; Sivavakkiyar asks why water in the mouth is called எச்சில் while the Veda churned in the same mouth is not.
links.teaches: The Siddhar turns the category the Acharakkovai uses to protect the brahmin against the brahmin's own recitation, showing that the purity rule depends on exempting the sacred mouth from it.

links.note: On the reading that புலை names the outcaste person, Acharakkovai 6 makes the sight of a birth-group polluting; Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from deeds.
links.teaches: The conflict holds only if புலை is a person and செய்தொழில் means conduct, so the pairing shows how the caste force of each verse rests on one disputed word.
links.list_adds: It sets a birth-group beside a dog and the heavenly bodies as one class of barred sights, a ranking by birth the Kural's verse denies.

links.note: Acharakkovai 7 classes sexual union and eating as kinds of எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the pure body itself came from எச்சில், and honey and milk are எச்சில் too.
links.teaches: The Siddhar takes the Acharakkovai's own classing of union as எச்சில் to its end: if union pollutes, every body and every food is born of pollution and the category cannot separate clean from unclean.

links.note: Acharakkovai 8 bars recitation while in எச்சில்; Sivavakkiyar says the mantra one recites is itself the mouth's எச்சில்.
links.teaches: One text guards recitation from impurity and the other calls recitation impure in itself, so the rule that protects the mantra is the Siddhar's evidence that purity of the mouth is a fiction.

links.note: Verse 7 defines the four kinds of எச்சில்; verse 8 says what they bar and what keeping them yields.
links.teaches: The pair shows the book's method: a definition followed by its prohibitions and a reward in learning, so purity rules are presented as a discipline of the scholar.

links.note: Kural 298 says water gives only outer purity and inner purity is seen through truth; Acharakkovai 10 lists ten occasions when water must remove impurity.
links.teaches: The Kural concedes the outer purity that the Acharakkovai regulates but makes it the lesser half, so the ten baths answer a question the Kural treats as minor; they are different things, not a contradiction.
links.list_adds: It turns the Kural's single clause on outer purity into an exact list of the occasions that call for a bath, among them dream, hair-cutting and contact with low people.

links.note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
links.teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.

links.note: Kural 1066 says asking even water for a cow degrades the tongue; Acharakkovai 12 says the worthy do not beg sandals even when they lack them.
links.teaches: The Acharakkovai brings the Kural's limit case of begging down to one's own bodily need and sets it inside a list of purity rules, so not begging becomes part of bodily propriety.
links.list_adds: It places the refusal to beg beside rules against touching oil and others' cloth, treating begging as a kind of defilement.

links.note: Both verses bar the sight of புலை, verse 6 to one in எச்சில், verse 13 to one who has oiled the body.
links.teaches: The bar on seeing புலை recurs under two different ritual states, which shows it is a standing rule of the code rather than a feature of one kind of impurity.

links.note: Acharakkovai 15 says one who scorns brahmins perishes; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth itself is ruined when his conduct fails.
links.teaches: The Kural adds the condition the Acharakkovai leaves out: reverence owed to the brahmin by birth lapses with his conduct, so the two books disagree on whether birth alone commands it.
links.list_adds: It sets brahmins with the elements, the cow, the sun and the moon as cosmic things owed reverence, a rank the Kural makes conditional on conduct.

links.note: Acharakkovai 16 makes the teacher one of five elders to be worshipped as gods; Purananuru 183 says learning is worth serving and paying the teacher, and that learning outweighs both seniority and the order of birth.
links.teaches: Puram 183 gives the reason for the teacher's place and also cuts against the list: the elder brother the Acharakkovai reveres yields to the wiser younger, and a learned man of the lowest order draws the highest to him.

links.note: Kural 942 regulates the meal by digestion, eating only after the last meal is spent; Acharakkovai 20 regulates it by direction, posture, silence and worship.
links.teaches: The two books divide the same act between body and rite: the Kural cares when and how much one eats, the Acharakkovai how one sits and where one looks, and neither addresses the other's concern.
links.list_adds: It makes the meal a sequence of bodily disciplines, facing east, stillness, silence and worship, none of which concerns the food itself.

new_concepts.gloss: rule-bound conduct; the codified rules of daily, bodily and ritual behaviour

source_issues: Verse 2 line 4 reads ஒழக்கம், most likely ஒழுக்கம் miswritten.

Verses 4 and 11 close with the same line (என்பதே முந்தையோர் கண்ட முறை), and verse 19 line 3 recurs at verse 42: a formulaic close of the work, flagged by the tool as a repeated line, not a corruption.
Verse 10 says ten (ஈரைந்தும்) but the tenth occasion is only reached by splitting ஊண்பொழுது from வைகு துயில்; ஏனை மயலுறல் is obscure.
Verse 13 lines 3-4 on oil and water are hard to order; the sense of நீர்தொடார் after oiling is unclear.
